title: Factorial Trailing Zeroes
summary: Determine the count of trailing zeroes in the factorial of a given integer n, where n! represents the product of all positive integers up to n.
statement: Determine the count of trailing zeroes in the factorial of a given integer n, where n! represents the product of all positive integers up to n.
constraints: Count only consecutive zero digits at the end of n!, not zeroes elsewhere in its decimal representation. Aim for logarithmic time without constructing n!.
hints: A trailing zero comes from a factor of ten, formed by a two and a five.
Factorials contain more factors of two than five; count every factor of five.
Add floor(n/5), floor(n/25), floor(n/125), and so on, stopping when the quotient becomes zero.
Repeated integer division by five computes those quotients without constructing the large factorial.
editorial: Each multiple of five contributes at least one factor of five; multiples of 25 contribute another, and similarly for higher powers. There are enough twos to pair with all those fives, so their total determines the trailing zero count. The independent oracle builds the exact factorial for small inputs and repeatedly removes decimal zeroes with division by ten. Seeded comparisons cover n up to 500; the 10000 boundary is checked against 2000+400+80+16+3=2499 directly.

tests.explanation: 3! is 6, whose decimal representation has no trailing zeroes.
There are five multiples of 5 up to 25, and 25 supplies one additional factor of 5: the answer is 6, not 5.
